Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that simplifies the unit commitment problem by reducing unnecessary constraints, thereby increasing solution times. Previous efforts have focused on multi-period validation, but this approach is computationally expensive and delays critical scheduling times. This paper introduces a more efficient validation method, called periodic validation, specifically targeting large-scale unit commitment problems with a large number of periods. By performing validation on a per-period basis, with consecutive periods examined sequentially, the method effectively reduces computational costs by bypassing unnecessary constraints. Experimental results confirm that the periodic validation method outperforms the multi-period method and significantly shortens solution times for the unit commitment problem. Furthermore, the method integrates seamlessly with existing solvers and constraints without necessitating code modifications. As such, it can be readily incorporated into modern constraint screening frameworks to enhance solution times for large-scale unit commitment problems. As a key advantage, the method is parallelizable in computational processing, allowing solution times to be significantly diminished when processed on high-performance computing architectures, such as GPUs, which can accelerate solution times by at least one order of magnitude. Demonstrative examples are available online in interactive HTML code, allowing readers to visualize the method's efficiency. This material can be accessed at https://share.shuangshi.fyi/apps/UnitCommitmentConstraintScreening/. To fill this knowledge gap, the present paper implements an innovative Multinomial Logit model, leveraging the discrete choice experiment method to quantify bicycle usage preferences. Notably, the proposed framework takes into account the inherent connections between environmental factors and ridership choices. Empirical evaluation of the developed model is performed by aggregating nearly 4000 discrete choice responses from a survey of cycling enthusiasts. Find out more at https://pslrx.github.io. Data and code for this study can be accessed at this link. In contrast to previous studies, the present research distinguishes between three distinct bicycle categories (conventional, assisted, and truly electric) and incorporates novel factors such as gross weight, range anxiety, and battery lifespan as key attributes. According to the findings, the primary factors influencing bicycle usage are financial considerations, anxiety regarding cycling and battery lifespan. Furthermore, the study reveals that conventional e-bikes are preferred over conventional bicycles, while there is surprisingly little preference for truly electric bicycles over e-bikes. Notably, the results suggest an increase in preferred bicycle distance in urban settings but remain consistent despite a substantial rise in road density and the presence of other vehicles. Finally, the study shows that financial considerations and range anxiety have a substantial impact on urban versus non-urban cycling, with financial considerations being the most influential factor. Nonetheless, the study finds that individuals who cyclically prefer e-bikes tend to set a maximum distance, fail to recharge their e-bikes even when their battery level falls below 90%, and tend to be hesitant to engage in long trips exceeding 40 miles without first assessing the route. Interestingly, the study results demonstrate that e-bike adoption is more pronounced among cyclists who cyclically prefer e-bikes, indicating that providing information about urban route lengths may be an effective strategy to promote the use of conventional bicycles over e-bikes. Furthermore, the results suggest that removing range anxiety may have a more pronounced impact on urban cycling distance than equipping existing conventional bicycles with electric assistance. However, the study results suggest that truly electric bicycles are unlikely to gain significant traction and should not be a primary focus of policy initiatives aimed at promoting sustainable cycling. Instead, the results indicate that promoting conventional e-bikes may be the key to increasing cycling distances in urban settings and thus enhancing air quality. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings and ReLU functions, has inherent limitations in representing certain nonlinear functions. Consequently, the ability of deep neural networks with this architecture to withstand sophisticated attacks is significantly diminished. These limitations not only apply to networks using batch normalization, but also those employing batch normalization alternatives such as Layer Normalization and Group Normalization. In contrast, deep networks using learning without regularization or incorporating linear layers are better equipped to handle robust attacks. These findings contribute new insights into the capabilities and constraints of neural networks, and underscore the importance of systematizing the analysis of neural network capabilities and limitations to enhance our understanding of machine learning. These results also imply that quantative assessments of adversarial robustness defenses are problematic due to varying network instantiations and training procedures. Ultimately, overcoming the limitations of neural networks is crucial to further advancements in adversarial robustness research. To address this challenge, we propose a simple training procedure to achieve perturbation robustness without compromising accuracy. However, achieving perturbation robustness is often at the expense of loss of model accuracy, and further advancements still require. From a practical standpoint, our proposal performs comparably to state-of-the-art approaches for robust training methods. From a theoretical perspective, this work lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive analysis of neural network capabilities and limitations, and aims to stimulate research in the field of adversarial machine learning. Moreover, by quantitatively measuring the expressiveness of neural networks, we are able to evaluate the effectiveness of different training procedures and network architectures. These findings can be leveraged to inform the design of neural networks and guide future advancements in machine learning design. Despite the efforts of various researchers, the creation of such neural networks remains a difficult task. We hope that the insights presented in this research can contribute to the development of novel algorithms and innovative solutions to the challenge of adversarial robustness. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. A practical demonstration is available at https://replaydl.github.io/VERF/. The source code can be found at https://github.com/replaydl/VERF. Additionally, we applied this framework to a problem of autonomous navigation for a robot, accessing a large-scale, continuously evolving observation space due to infinite variability in traffic conditions over time. The results show that VERF optimizes the robot's navigation strategy approximately 2.73 times faster than professional human drivers and the current best state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Furthermore, the paper discusses how VERF may be used to resolve some challenges in reinforcement learning, such as efficiently multi-task learning and learning from limited data. In particular, the paper suggests prioritizing observations that are far from the current optimal control point during the initial learning phase to effectively explore the parameter space when optimizing a predefined reward function. Moreover, to boost the effectiveness of free exploration from random rewards when the reward function is unknown, the paper suggests prioritizing observations with high correlation to past historical data once the function approximator's noise has been quantified. We have conducted a practical demonstration in a popular deep reinforcement learning benchmark to showcase the efficacy of these ideas. The results show that VERF successfully learns to drive like a normal person and the derived experience replay framework is robust across different driving models and increasingly challenging scenarios. We have shared our findings with researchers working on learning to drive from video streams and the VERF framework may also contribute to advancements in other complex, dynamic systems and the reinforcement learning domain in general. This study examines the automatic promotion problem, seeking to detect untouched subcategories that are logically incorporated into their parent categories within large taxonomies. Prior research has shown that statistical correlation between category descriptions and user inquiries can serve as a foundation for this promotion problem. However, this approach is only as accurate as the level of descriptive variability among categories, which may otherwise overlook relevant promotions. Therefore, we present a novel technique that leverages semantic differences between categories, specifically their subcategory compositions, to supplement the correlation evidence. The presented research introduces the NDT-Transformer approach, enabling real-time, large-scale place recognition using 3D point clouds. The methodology utilizes the 3D Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation to summarize dense point clouds into easier-to-compute distributions, facilitating efficient similarity comparisons. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed. Counting can be solved via two beeps from any two close stations, allowing for $O(1)$ exact counts and $O(d/\log^2n)$ time in weighted balls and chains protocols, where $n$ is the number of stations and $d$ is the gelbaum number. Meanwhile, naming takes $O(h+\log^2n)$ time with existing protocols for exact distances, but we've developed new protocols that reach $O(\log^2n)$ time and $O(\log n)$ energy usage. Counting can also be solved with $O(d)$ time and $O(d)$ energy usage using any distance oracle, and naming can be solved with $O(\mathcal{H}^2)$ time and $O(\mathcal{H}^2)$ energy usage where $\mathcal{H}$ is the height of the naming tree. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents areas where the model's prediction diverges from its true label. By recognizing this, we separate pseudo-labels from actual labels and assign them different weights to their respective supervised objectives. The theoretical underpinnings of our method involve optimizing neighborhood entropy to generate informative pseudo-labels, while pruning unnecessary nodes to prevent data degradation. Experimental results on various graph datasets indicate that our proposed method, InfoGNN, outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving the highest accuracy using a limited number of labels. This research examines how differences in the plasma's radial dimensions and off-center electron injection affect the resulting beam dynamics and betatron radiation spectra emitted by witness electron particles in proton-driven plasmas. By analyzing these dynamics, the study demonstrates the potential for uncovering initial conditions of witness electron bunches and injected proton bunches. It also explores the feasibility of using betatron radiation spectroscopy to track the growing self-modulation of intense proton beams in the presence of self-trapped electron bubbles in the plasmas. Furthermore, the research shows that modifying the plasma's central electron content can either enhance or suppress the growth of electron bubbles and concomitantly the high-frequency components of the radiation spectra. Consequently, the study recommends that to optimize the detection of useful high-frequency betatron radiation in the AWAKE-like setup, the plasma should be filled with a minimum of electrons. Moreover, the growth of electron bubbles can be prevented or suppressed by introducing self-ejectile bubbles that reduce the scale of the electron bunches, thereby shrinking the potential acceleration gaps and their associated radiation spectra. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of plasma-driven electron acceleration and highlights the complexities and universality of the underlying physics, which could have significant implications for the design of future compact photon sources. Finally, the study presents a conceptual design for a compact, plasma-based, free-electron laser involving the seeding of a bunch of low-charge electrons in a small plasma column to investigate the transfer of energy from the electrons to the photons. This design could provide a novel approach to the development of extremely compact yet high-powered laser sources with potential industrial applications. Future experimental research intent on demonstrating the findings of this research is currently under consideration at the University of Mainz. These skills remain useful even across significantly different targets and environments, and the agents can successfully accomplish tasks that previously proved insurmountable for individual agents, despite being more complex and demanding. Plants reacting to external stimuli offer a practical application of reinforcement learning in real-world settings, offering a plethora of challenges in the areas of dynamics, reward functions, and noisy sensor input. However, solving the complexities of open-loop growth, such as determining when to bloom, leaf, or reproduce, poses a significant barrier to entry for reinforcement learning algorithms. Experimental results show a notable improvement in fitness across all three stages of learning - growth plan optimization, reinforcement learning tuning of the high-level plan, and reinforcement learning tuning of the low-level plant pose. Our research demonstrates the practical implications of reinforcement learning applying to real-world problems, particularly in the complex domain of biology. Furthermore, the utilization of artificial growth plans enables the seamless integration of biology and machine learning, eliminating the requirement for plant-specific domain expertise to be introduced into the system. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic pre-trained model with a finely-tuned model. By combining these two methods, we were able to improve the episode accuracy and overall performance of RockNet and enhance the robustness of RockBlocks to future episodes. Additionally, we were able to demonstrate the superiority of our approach to standard techniques in the field of continual learning by conducting an ablation study, which highlighted the potential of our framework for future research. Ultimately, the simplicity of RockNet makes it an attractive candidate for addressing a range of challenges in both continual learning and multi-task learning. However, the quality of the resulting approximation can severely degrade if the vector's components have significant squared values. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel "correction-aware" approach for CountSketch, which modifies the algorithm with orthogonal matrices and incorporates feedback from the host vector. We provide an analytical framework for determining the accuracy of this revised method and conduct experimental evaluations to compare its performance to alternative techniques such as SPC and JLS. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using artificial datasets and a real-world example involving diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal images. The findings show that the Euler characteristic can be used to monitor changes in complex, multi-variable spaces and that it may provide clear results, especially when combining different thresholds for classification purposes. Furthermore, the Euler characteristic can be calculated quickly, and the additional time needed for mapping and computation is often negligible. We conclude that while the Euler characteristic may not offer precise differences for similar conditions, it can effectively track changes and help reduce noise, especially when using machine learning algorithms. Using the Euler characteristic can simplify the explanation of these models and improve noise reduction in multi-variable spaces. Our analysis shows that the Euler characteristic-based feature reduction outperformed homogeneous feature selection in predicting diabetic retinopathy. Utilizing Euler characteristic for feature selection or reduction has the advantages of offering clear interpretations, reducing noise, and gaining computational efficiency. We believe that combining the Euler characteristic with machine learning models represents a promising strategy for analyzing complex systems. The implementation of this method is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/vazquezpa/eztop. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, we establish that a condition similar to high-frequency validity does exist, enabling the definition of a effective Floquet Liouvillian and its convergence guarantee, based on the expansion of the time-evolution operator of the driving bath. We further investigate the series expansion of the Floquet Liouvillian by conjugation, relating it to the driven open quantum system's steady states and its convergence to the asymptotic behavior of the system. In a more general case of multiple energy levels, we explore numerically the precision of the approximations for the Floquet Liouvillian generated by different driving protocols, comparing them to numerical solutions of the time-dependent master equation that does not rely on additional assumptions. In addition, frequency-smoothing techniques are also investigated and combined with the high-frequency expansion, resulting in the reconstruction of the Floquet steady states of the open quantum system for valid conditions, based on the existence of periodic Floquet steady states. Our study provides a framework to validate the applicability and precision of the high-frequency approximations for driving protocols with low noise and high modulation rate. In systems with non-commuting driving Hamiltonian and non-markovian dynamics, a different approach is required, and we make a preliminary analysis, proposing a numerical method to solve the high-frequency approximation for open quantum systems, by relating it to a effective driven quantum optic chain problem. In this new framework, we show that there exists a condition for validity of the high-frequency expansion that depends on the system and bath interactions, and obtain numerically the periodic steady states of the time-asymptotic open quantum system for valid cases. In a more general case of non-markovian dynamics, we show that there exists a condition of validity of the high-frequency expansion for a wide class of quantum systems and bath dynamics, and propose a numerical method to solve the high-frequency expansion for non-markovian dynamics, by relating it to a non-linear problem of a classical optical parametric amplifier, and study the precision and applicability of the high-frequency expansion for different protocols of driving and decoherence. Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methods and increasing
computational capabilities enable the extraction of formal logical structures from
natural language inputs with growing precision and breadth.
  This research outlines a formal framework for utilizing Hoare logic in the
formal verification of imperative programs through logical structures derived from
compositional semantic parsing of declarative language assertions.
Our proposed method, dubbed Natural Hoare Logic, enables direct software
verification against domain-specific safety requirements specified in everyday
language.
  This paper presents the results of a domain-specific, end-to-end testing
effort from natural language to formal verification, demonstrating the feasibility
of utilizing both compositional semantic parsing and Hoare logic to provide
formal assurances for critical system functionalities. The testing initiative
focused on safety requirements within a realistic, real-time navigation
environment drawn from a popular in-vehicle navigation system.
  To illustrate the applicability of domain-specific, compositional semantic
parsing to formal verification processes, this paper includes two additional, more
intricate logic demonstrations, showcasing increasingly complex
domain-specific functionalities. Furthermore, the paper discusses the advantages
of employing natural language-based software assertions over traditional
countermatrix assertions. Our findings suggest that Natural Hoare Logic can be
effectively employed not only in formal verification but also in automated testing
and logical reasoning. 
  The software verification process described here achievement is a milestone
for using natural language-based assertions and affirming the feasibility of
utilizing composable, semantic parses for supporting diverse, logical
reasonings. Our forward-looking analysis reveals that Natural Hoare Logic can
further facilitate automated reasoning and logical computations for numerous
reasoning tasks, including both natural language and computer-based systems.

Notably, winners of the challenge solved the problem by transforming the task into a classification issue, using CNNs to identify local features, and then a LSTM network for predicting future states. 
We will tackle the challenge from a different angle, training a multi-task learning model that combines three objectives: forecasting traffic volume and speed at a given city, and predicting their corresponding errors. 
Along the way, we will employ data augmentation techniques that simplify the transition from training on a small subset of the data to any city.

Entity Recognition (FG-NER) involves identifying and categorizing various entity types, typically ranging from 50 to several hundred, by precise fine-grained categorization. In general, FG-NER exhibits characteristics similar to both traditional named entity recognition and fine-grained classification, with the first aspect requiring model designs that can effectively extract entities and the second aspect allowing for the incorporation of numerous additional labels. In our study, we observed that general-purpose language models, when trained on labeled data in a sequence-labeling framework, such as FG-NER, can overcome the challenge of extracting entities to a considerable extent. Furthermore, to address the second aspect, we implemented a unique label-distribution strategy that adapts to the unique characteristics of FG-NER by incorporating multiple local labels into the training process through the utilization of multi-head attention mechanisms in transformer models. By distributing the labels in this manner, the model is able to learn to rely equally on the labeled data and therefore incorporate the information contained within the additional labels into the training process in a parallel fashion. Our experiments with both single-model and ensemble approaches based on the unique label-distribution strategy achieved state-of-the-art performance in the 2016-2017 CoNLL FG-NER task. Our results demonstrate that effective FG-NER can be achieved to a considerable extent by leveraging a general-purpose language model and incorporating the unique characteristics of the task, including the number of entity categories and labels, into the training process. Our implementation of the unique label-distribution strategy can be accessed through the repository at https://github.com/jongwonlee FG-NER. Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. This study focuses on the GCR's dimensions, thermodynamic efficiency, and electrical output to determine the minimum fuel requirements and assessment of the system's performance under various operational conditions. A novel approach to integrating the GCR with the magnetohydrodynamic generator allows for enhanced efficiency and reduced energy losses, as demonstrated by numerical simulations and experimental data obtained from the HOMER magnetohydrodynamic generator prototype. By combining the GCR and magnetohydrodynamic generator, a self-sustaining power system is achieved, converting nuclear energy into electrical power required for space travel. Using the results from a NASA-designed spacecraft, the Kriegler mission, our findings quantify how different GCR configurations impact mission success based on their dimensions and thermodynamic efficiency. This analysis provides critical design specifications and operational guidelines for integrating the GCR and magnetohydrodynamic generator in nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space travel. Additionally, a detailed examination of the HOMER prototype reveals opportunities to optimize its design based on lessons from historical magnetohydrodynamic generators and the development of a modern direct conversion device, the spin glaze photovoltaic device. This innovative design allows for the conversion, amplification, and transmission of electrical energy through the rotation of ferromagnetic seeds in a vacuum, overcoming the limited range of magnetohydrodynamic generators by reducing their size while increasing their electrical output. This technology provides a promising alternative to traditional solar cells that require a significant curved surface to collect light, a major drawback that the spin glaze photovoltaic generator overcomes by enabling compact, flat designs that are both efficient and efficient. Using the Kriegler mission as a reference, the spin glaze photovoltaic generator is evaluated for its performance and efficiency and found to deliver high-quality purified water to NASA's astronauts.

We explore two specific scenarios: one focusing on the relationship between bulk and corner states, and the other examining corner-state correlations. We establish the existence of mobility gaps for bulk-corner connections and show that while bulk-corner correlations decay with distance, corner-corner correlations exhibit no significant distance effects, given finite size constraints. These findings are supported through both analytical and numerical analyses of a corresponding lattice model. We leverage our results to discover an unusual phenomenon: while bulk-corner connections exhibit a topological phase transition as the disorder strength increases, the bulk-corner and corner-corner connections show no such transition within the finite size scope. Additionally, the corner-state and bulk-corner correlations display non-ergodic behavior with increased disorder, exhibiting multi-component structures. We obtain corner-state entanglement spectra, revealing the origin of non-ergodicity and its relationship with topological properties. Specifically, the bulk-corner and corner-corner entanglement spectra both exhibit bulk-corner zero modes as a unique feature. Based on this, we propose a method for identifying bulk-corner zero modes and bulk-corner singularities in the two-point correlation function. These methods are applied to different lattice models, confirming the existence of such singularities in time or frequency domains for various disorder potentials. These results are highly versatile and applicable to a broader range of systems beyond the specific Su(2) topological insulators studied here. They are particularly relevant for understanding non-ergodic behavior, and bulk-corner and corner-corner correlations in various applications, including higher-order topological insulators, quantum Hall systems, and cold atoms. Furthermore, the application of bulk-corner singularities as a probe for singularities within the frequency domain warrants further exploration in the study of quasiperiodic systems. As an example, the application of bulk-corner singularities in the study of quantum chaos is also discussed in the conclusion section. Finally, the conclusion section also discusses a possible experimental realization of the features studied here, such as in a Bose-Hubbard model with additional superfluid background. To this end, the features studied here may be realized through a mixture of two-component bosons with a superfluid background in an optical lattice. An immediate potential extension of this work involves the study of bulk-corner singularities in the time domain, corresponding to a quantum chaotic Hamiltonian with finite time evolution. constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as operations. However, with the shift to "next-generation" services featuring immersive, real-world operations, we find a significant gap between these high-level interfaces and the underlying execution logic necessary to connect them. Existing standards and technologies like OpenAPI and HTTP APIs struggle to adequately capture the complexities of real-world operations, necessitating a new approach to service orchestration suited for modern "next-generation" services. This requires a more detailed and nuanced understanding of service interfaces, beyond what current standards provide. As a result, advanced annotation and modeling are necessary to facilitate the creation of complex distributed systems, prompting the need for a more sophisticated, high-level architecture for service orchestration, filling this overlooked requirement. This paper introduces a concept for a service orchestration framework, specifically tailored for "next-generation" services, which bridges the existing knowledge gap between these high-level interfaces and the underlying execution logic. The framework's implementation is explained, along with a practical evaluation of its capabilities in real-world settings. Through this implementation, we demonstrate the efficacy of a higher-level service orchestration framework in filling the existing knowledge gap between "next-generation" service interfaces and the underlying execution logic, encompassing both data and execution management. The practical implications and advantages of this implementation are discussed, highlighting its suitability for a wide range of applications and showcasing a tangible, impactful assessment of its usability in real-world settings, particularly in human visual processing and dermoscopy. The evaluation shows that a more sophisticated, high-level architecture for service orchestration can effectively connect various services and applications to the underlying execution logic, translating into substantial real-world benefits for users. Overall, this implementation marks an important milestone in bridging the significant knowledge gap between "next-generation" service interfaces and the underlying execution logic, ushering in a new era of highly advanced, high-quality distributed systems and highlighting the immense potential of next-generation services in the realm of service-oriented computing. The implementation of this architecture is freely accessible for further development and improvement. The associated source code is available at https://github.com/DermAttractors/service-orchestration-next-gen. The project's documentation is at https://next-gen-service-orchestration.readthedocs.io/, while the paper's official publication can be found at https://doi.org/10.3390/services2022020008. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing the frustration caused by delayed arrivals. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights gained from problem analysis to incorporate various cutting plane and branching techniques. To improve computational efficiency, a accelerated branch-and-cut method is also introduced, ensuring the solver can effectively address extremely large-scale instances of the dial-a-ride problem in real-world applications. To test the solver's capabilities, extensive computational experiments were conducted on 504 highly structured instances of pool-based ridepooling services, yielding several key insights into what contributes to solvers encountering computational difficulties. Using these insights, a prediction model is developed to accurately forecast solve time for such pooled ridepooling instances, enabling service providers to adjust parameters to improve solver performance. We conclude this paper by presenting a weighted version of the dial-a-ride problem, offering potential avenues for future research in this domain. To facilitate future research, the proposed weighted dial-a-ride problem is incorporated into the CPAIB-DARPS library, which is accessible at https://github.com/franciscogonzal/CPAIB-DARPS. Additionally, the predictor is implemented in the form of a Python tool, available at https://github.com/franciscogonzal/pool-dar-predictor. Interestingly, despite the solver's accelerated branch-and-cut method, a number of the computed solver timings exceeded one hour, presenting an opportunity for future improvement. Consequently, the predictor tool is applied to compute predicted solve times for each of the computed timings, yielding an estimation of the potential performance improvement that could be achieved with the aid of more powerful computational tools, such as those proposed in https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12584. As an example, for 20 out of 119 computed timings, the predicted solve time is at least 90 minutes, with five expected to exceed 180 minutes, suggesting that enhancing computers or employing more advanced solving methods may be necessary to address medium to large-scale pooled ridepooling services optimally in the near future. Nevertheless, this solver, although slow for some instances, is still capable of computing high-quality lower and upper bounds for dial-a-ride problems with pool-based ridepooling services within a reasonable amount of time (24 hours). We anticipate that the Branch-and-Cut algorithm, paired with more powerful computers or future improvements, will be able to compute optimal solutions efficiently in the future.

A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier work focusing on a unified prediction with multiple kernels. Our approach accurately reflects the predictive capabilities of individual layers and enables the evaluation of their unique contributions. Experimentation with datasets CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 supports the value of layer-specific kernels over a unified model, possibly paving the way for the incorporation of our method in more efficient learning strategies or tasks like object recognition in video data. Furthermore, by analyzing the layer kernels, we observed that the first layer's predictive feature weights frequently resulted in diminished or irrelevant features for the task at hand, potentially serving as an useful feature reduction technique. Ultimately, our work suggests that utilizing multiple neural tangent kernels to interpret deep neural networks may provide insights into various aspects of network design. At the time of submission, the code used for our research remains under development and will be made available for review. It is our hope that the code will also facilitate the replication of studies focusing on neural tangent kernels as a means to improve interpretability in deep learning. The underlying C definitions and ACL2 definitions for this example are available online, along with the corresponding proof verification scripts. Furthermore, a separate document provides an overview of the design decisions that guided the development of this new approach to trustworthy software systems. A series of finite state machine-based examples of verified C functions, which implement the rules for decimal arithmetic as specified in Theorem 10.6.21 of the ACL2 Users Guide, are used to demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel methodology. The first such function, dec-plus, represents an implementation of the "+" operation for decimal arithmetic, and the accompanying theorem, +ondec-objects, verifies its correctness. The second function, dec-times, corresponds to the "+" operation for decimal objects, and the accompanying theorem, timesondec-objects, confirms the correctness of this implementation. The third function, dec-equal, serves as an implementation of the "=" function for decimal objects, and the accompanying theorem, equalondec-objects, verifies its correctness. The remaining three functions, corresponding to the special forms of "+" and "-", as specified in decimal object theory, are implemented in the following sections. The first set of functions, +and-, is used to implement the "+" and "-" operations on decimal objects, and the accompanying theorems verify their correctness. This study investigates the potential of incorporating domain knowledge into a model, specifically a multivariate linear regression trained on a dataset of films spanning 2004-2014. The study also demonstrates a technique for extracting a movie's characteristics from text, utilizing natural language processing and feature extraction. This capability allows filmmakers to gauge how similar new movies are to established ones and make informed decisions about production. In an actual case study, researchers analyzed the 2016 films 'Captain America: Civil War' and 'Star Trek Beyond' to illustrate the practical application of the model. The model predicts 'Captain America: Civil war''s box-office earnings with high precision but identifies 'Star Trek Beyond' as a poorly made film due to its negative critical reception and low runtime. However, incorporating domain knowledge reveals that both films could have been saved by increasing their respective budgets above $200 million. Furthermore, using the model in conjunction with domain knowledge, it appears that another poorly received film, 'Solo: A Star Wars Story,' would have been more successful with a longer runtime. In conclusion, the model's predictions are grounded in actionable advice for filmmakers, achievable through modifications such as adjusting production features. This, in turn, allows filmmakers to make well-informed decisions and give themselves an edge over their competitors. Weighted bipartite graphs can effectively represent transactions between
financial accounts, making maximum matching a suitable operation for classifying
financial records. However, this approach has limitations when dealing with
record discrepancies. Account anomalies can arise from invalid or unregistered
account relationships. Focusing on the US Federal Reserve's financial transactions,
our research develops an efficient system combining bipartite graph analysis and
maximum matching to detect anomalies in the transactions. The findings show that
our method substantially reduces processing time, achieving speedup of over 200
times compared to existing solutions, while maintaining linear space complexity. 
The proposed method yields similar results for the purposes of categorization.

significant task in various fields, including motion detection and attribute
definition. In the absence of a complete temporal pattern, as is the case for US

challenge. The proposed ANOMYPy box detection framework is a robust tool for
initial anomaly identification and localization in sequential time series data.

and employs dynamic programming to determine activity intervals that are
completely or partially present in the data sequence. The framework provides
support for the synchronization of data from different sources and is capable of
producing a visual representation of the anomalies, enabling their further
analysis in further research. The discovery of anomalies in the Federal Reserve

However, the current tools provide an overabundance of suggestions, making it challenging for developers to prioritize these improvements with their limited resources, as implementing all suggestions is impractical. Since developers cannot apply all suggestions due to time constraints, they typically select a single suggestion at a time from the list provided by the tool, which may lead to relevant suggestions being overlooked, as they are never re-evaluated due to the persistent nature of the codebase.

To address this issue, our novel tool, ms-code-suggestions, offers developers with a dynamic and dynamic A/B testing-capable interface to receive relevant code suggestions, which are re-evaluated as they are being applied to the codebase, as well as prioritize these suggestions based on their perceived usefulness, which is updated as the developer interacts with the tool. Additionally, our tool provides the option to include relevant information, such as file name and location, to enhance the overall experience of receiving code suggestions. ms-code-suggestions is implemented using Next.js, a modern React.js framework, which also incorporates dynamic A/B testing to allow developers to experiment with new features and suggestions without disrupting existing tool usage, as the tool can be easily integrated or tested on existing IDE-integrated platforms. ms-code-suggestions is currently available for testing at https://ms-cs.net/. As a practical application of our tool, we performed an A/B testing experiment, which demonstrated that prioritiizing code suggestions based on their perceived relevance results in a 10.3% higher likelihood that developers actually apply the suggestions, as evaluating the effectiveness of this feature yields an 83.7% matching rate with the developers' stated preferences. Despite the relatively small-scale testing, this evidence suggests that prioritiizing code suggestions based on their perceived relevance can lead to increased actual implementation rates, as implementing this feature results in a higher likelihood of relevant suggestions being applied to the codebase. As a secondary contribution to the field of software engineering, we performed an extensive review of existing code suggestion tools, which identified 31 tools, as there seems to be a lack of clear guidelines on the features that make up a modern, good code suggestion tool, as the identified tools lack uniformity in their overall performance and even basic functionality like code analysis and suggestion generation. In light of this observation, we took on the challenge of filling this knowledge gap by systematizing the features of a good code suggestion tool,

rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic frequencies. This response is due to a phenomenon called "cavitation," where high-frequency sound waves create voids within the gel, altering its mechanical properties in a predictable manner. To date, the full potential of rheo-acoustic gels remains unknown. Using a combination of experimental measurements and computer simulations, scientists have found that applying ultrasonic energy near the gel's glass transition temperature leads to the formation of stable micro-scale voids. These voids become stable due to the consistent impact of the ultrasonic waves at the gel's surface. Initially, the voids resemble a spherical shape, but they evolve into an elliptical shape resembling an American football due to the imbalance of stresses. The presence of these voids triggers a thermodynamic instability, causing the gel to transition into a state of increased porosity. This new state of rheo-acoustic gels exhibits mechanical properties that include elastic behavior similar to that of fractured solids, along with frictional surface interactions. The formation of these rheo-acoustic gels with micro-scale voids breaks new ground in soft-matter research and has significant implications for the development of unique soft-matter technologies. This innovative work also sheds light on the impact of frictional contact forces in the early stages of gel formation. Rheo-acoustic gels have the potential to be used in a range of practical applications, including the processing of gels, the creation of soft-matter solids with controllable fracture properties, and the development of soft-matter phononic crystals, all of which were simulated but have not yet been experimentally confirmed. Additional research is required to realize these potential applications. An experimental validation of the concept is currently in progress in our lab. within a particular field, precise categorization of document subjects is crucial. Currently, classification primarily relies on human expertise, but semi-supervised Machine Learning algorithms can aid this process by utilizing labeled data to predict subject classes for previously uncategorized documents. Despite their assistance, these machine-driven classifications often lack clarity as they usually generate a single main class and secondary categories. Recent research, however, has shown promise in applying clustering algorithms to improve subject organization and documentation readability, by assigning primary and secondary categories to the same set of documents. This paper aims to compare four popular unsupervised learning approaches (K-Means, Hierarchical Clustering, Self-Organizing Maps, and Latent Semantic Analysis) using a shared dataset and evaluation criteria, in order to determine which method excels at facilitating document classification and subject organization. Our evaluation shows that all methods produce comparable results, with each approach offering benefits and drawbacks; however, due to its high speed, ease of interpretation, and performance, K-Means appears to be the most suitable option for document classification. To demonstrate the potential of this method, we applied K-Means to a dataset of classified documents and generated a Subject Hierarchical Taxonomy (SHTree), which retains the effectiveness of document classification while introducing a more transparent and easily browsable subject hierarchy. Our results show that using SHTree instead of a flat list of classifications enhances navigation and provides an additional organizational benefit. This paper concludes that employing a multi-faceted subject classification system, comprising a hierarchical structure with main and secondary categories, is more suitable for document classification and rendering large digital collections more accessible. Consequently, the introduced Subject Hierarchical Taxonomy represents a viable alternative to traditional classification methods and offers additional benefits in terms of documentation readability and navigation. This paper serves as a starting point for future research into various hierarchical structures and welcomes contributions to this area of study. To facilitate reproducibility and promote research in this area, the used dataset and implemented SHTree code have been made publicly available. Documentation and classification are closely intertwined, and recent advances in Machine Learning have made it possible to utilize automatically assigned classifications to aid human experts in their work. This paper compares various document classification methods and introduces a new approach, the Subject Hierarchical Taxonomy, which retains the effectiveness of machine-driven classifications while introducing a more transparent and easily browsable subject hierarchy. Using the SHARE dataset and a range of evaluation criteria, the paper shows that the proposed SHTree outperforms flat classifications and offers additional benefits in terms of documentation readability and navigation. QL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for automating SPARQL query generation, but these models have a major limitation: they can only handle queries based on knowledge that was learned during training. When encountering questions about new knowledge resources, classes, or properties, these models fall short, making them ineffective beyond their training scope. Leveraging the success achieved in other areas of natural language processing, we developed an innovative approach that involves introducing a mechanism to copy elements directly from questions. By integrating this 'copy mechanism' into established Seq2Seq models like CNNs and Transformers, we can significantly boost their performance. We put this enhanced architecture to the test using state-of-the-art datasets containing questions about new knowledge elements. Compared to their standard counterparts, our results indicate substantial improvements across all datasets. Moreover, our approach delivers competitive performance when compared to more complex models that incorporate the copy mechanism. Given the established reputation of CNNs and the efficiency of the copy mechanism, we believe our architecture to be a reliable and effective solution for generating SPARQL queries. Consequently, our architecture presents a suitable baseline for future research in this domain. Using our approach, we also developed a method to extract knowledge relationships from question-answer pairs, resulting in a substantial expansion of the 15k question dataset. Nevertheless, manual examination reveals a considerable percentage of incorrect answers in the dataset. We propose that accurate machine learning-based answer verification could greatly accelerate the creation of large, high-quality question-answer pairs, ultimately facilitating the development of robust SPARQL query models. With this goal in mind, we implemented an algorithm using neural networks to verify answers in the 15k dataset, showing that it successfully identifies incorrect answers and significantly outperforms a basic model. Furthermore, our approach exhibits impressive real-world applicability by successfully translating over 180k SPARQL queries containing new knowledge elements that were gathered from a recent knowledge-based question-answering competition. By doing so, our approach sets a new record for highest accuracy in translating this type of data. All the code used for these experiments can be accessed through this GitHub repository. However, when dealing with sequential data such as streaming video, missing tensor entries need to be reconstructed in real-time without compromising performance. Existing streaming algorithms may not be effective when the data structure changes frequently, as in the case of missing chunks in video frames. Completing smaller chunks from previous frames and then filling in the missing tensor entries may not yield optimal results, particularly if the missing data involves chunks from previous frames. This paper presents a new tensor completion approach tailored for streaming video that minimizes memory and computation requirements. First, a full-rank tensor representation of each frame is computed and stored in a sketch. Then, to complete a chunk, it is combined with previous frames' sketches and a rank-minimization problem is solved. This approach can be further optimized by applying a solution specifically designed for online tensor completion. Experimental results show that our solution provides the best trade-off between reconstruction quality, memory usage, and computational speed among competing algorithms. Additionally, our technique outperforms existing streaming algorithms that use incremental Singular Value Decomposition. Furthermore, our new algorithm surpasses existing solutions designed for streaming data by using a different approach to solve the rank-minimization problem, achieving better reconstruction quality and computational speed. Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skeleton-based image representation allows for the
generation of images with varied viewpoints, while maintaining a predictable pattern
of appearance changes. In this paper, we propose an object representation approach,
combining a 3D skeleton with DNR, which can be learned from a limited number of image
captures. Our technique utilizes two neural components: a skeleton embedding network,
which encodes the object's shape and appearance from a few views, and a new DNR
component that stores view-dependent information as a linear combination of the
skeleton-based embeddings. The resulting linear representation enables accurate
reconstruction of new views and accurate transfer of appearance changes. Our method
exceeds state-of-the-art 3D deformation-based approaches in transferring appearance
across views and supports a significantly larger number of new views with high
precision. Furthermore, it requires minimal supervision and can produce realistic
results when trained on just one view. The associated code is available at
https://github.com/amirghadie/DNR-Skeleton.

Compared to our own internal object representations, which are more detailed, they fall short. Despite this, we find that ANNs with similar capabilities are better equipped to handle distorted objects than distorted versions of regular objects, which we observe to be harder for them to recognize. In contrast, we notice that ANNs exhibit a notable and consistent slow-down in processing times for a range of challenging object recognition tasks as the number of hidden layers within them increases. This anomaly indicates that overcomplex neural models may actually impair their performance and even result in processing delays. Ultimately, our research aims to gain a deeper understanding of ANN architecture and its implications for recognizing objects like our brains do. By leveraging computational tools to replicate annealing processes, we observe that replacing standard fully-connected ANNN layers with these newer architectures significantly improves our models' ability to identify both regular and distorted objects. This marked improvement is characterized by substantially lower classification errors and, perhaps more remarkably, their ability to recognize masked objects. Notably, these breakthroughs are accompanied by a notable and consistent speed-up in processing times. By mirroring key aspects of annealing processes, we observe that our novel ANNs are well-suited to recognizing detailed and distorted objects like our own internal object representations and humans' brains. In this context, we interpret annealing processes as a form of active learning, designed to facilitate the acquisition of new knowledge, which we have applied here in the context of object recognition. As ANNs are increasingly used throughout a range of domains to recognize objects and other items, we argue that incorporating details about distorted objects into our models could, in turn, improve our understanding of ANNs and human object recognition. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) before passing it through a neural network for a dimension-reduced representation. Notably, our model increases the h value to incorporate higher-order connectivity, but in sparse networks, higher-order interactions are less significant, which is acknowledged by our proof that decreases the model's error as h increases in these types of sparse networks. Our research further identifies and proves that decreasing the model's error is dependent on the convergence of the sequence of block diagonals of a Gram matrix constructed from the SNHAM, which is shown to be true for the first few iterations but may diverge and cease to converge in the following iterations. This is quantitatively validated by experiments on various sparse networks. Furthermore, our research extends the SSNE model to incorporate node attributes and improves its predictive capabilities by incorporating attribute-specified loss during training, which is supported by our empirical results on multiple sparse networks. Consequently, both predication accuracy and the resulting feature embeddings are enhanced. Notably, our research also illustrates that incorporating higher-order connectivity may be beneficial for predicting links in dense networks. Based on the SSNE model, our research further derives an algorithm for predicting link probabilities by applying a Poisson random field using the neural network's output and the predicted embeddings from the SSNE model, which is shown to outperform existing methods on multiple sparse networks. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, hampering efforts to enhance user experience. To address this gap, we've developed a multi-task learning approach, combining user behavior data with expert knowledge of user engagement drivers. We've labeled this approach LAR for "Latent Aspect Recreation." LAR separates user platform interactions into distinct categories, representing real-world factors that cause users to behave consistently. Experimental results on a large-scale production platform confirm that LAR can accurately decode users' underlying motivations, accurately predicting a wide range of subsequent platform interactions. By decoding users' motivations, LAR enables more effective future behavior predictions, surpassing the recommendation models currently used in production by significant margins. Furthermore, LAR's decoded latent factors provide valuable insights into user engagement drivers, making it a better all-around recommender than traditional sequential models. We've integrated LAR into a leading e-commerce platform, replacing the existing recommendation model to provide users with more personalized engagement. We've observed an increase in user satisfaction, measured by the number of subsequent platform interactions. We've demonstrated that this enhancement arises from improved visibility of in-app content, not simply increased overall engagement. We've found that understanding user engagement drivers is particularly crucial during in-app retention, as users are more receptive to tailored suggestions. We've developed a new in-app message approach, tailored to user motivation, to improve visibility and increase engagement during this critical phase. This approach has resulted in a significant 25.85% increase in selected in-app messages and an overall 14.82% boost in following in-app content. AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token combinations are widely demanded in the market.

In contrast, Automated Market Makers are accompanied by elevated trading volumes and liquidity provision by professional traders for token pairs exhibiting high demand. 
In contrast to the prevailing view that Automated Market Makers are utilized to introduce unexperienced tokens to new markets, the data suggests the opposite: Automated Market Makers are employed more frequently for token pairs that have established a user base. 
In particular, our research provides an interpretation of Automated Market Makers from the perspective of their users.

a phenomenon also observed in other decentralized applications.

annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than a single one. The proposed method can be viewed as a form of model ensemble that utilizes confidence to identify potential errors during the tagging process. Experimental findings indicate that the set-valued prediction framework can improve the accuracy of POS tagging on the 18th-19th century Scottish Gaelic Treebank from 73.48% to 74.13%. Notably, a secondary evaluation showed that set-valued tags can facilitate the annotation of verb-subject agreement in Scottish Gaelic, specifically with regards to the agreement between verb and subject- agreement marker. The set-valued tagging framework, as demonstrated on the Scottish Gaelic corpus, presents an innovative solution to the issues of unknown tags, ambiguous tags, and words with non-standard orthographies in historical text-based NLP problems. Moreover, it has the potential to be successfully applied to other similar linguistic datasets. Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously proposed powerspaces.  This paper also establishes that these new powerdomains fail to satisfy the demand for strong partial map continuity. Specifically, the convex powerspace fails to be embedded in the upper or lower powerspace for any directed space. Additionally, the construction of spaces that have the jumping property by using the convex, upper, or lower powerspace of a directed space is shown to fail. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. Our findings provide valuable insights into the relationship between the news industry's decline and shifting consumer behaviors, as well as the implications for U.S. local disease control strategies. In agreement with previous studies, our analysis also confirms that COVID coverage was motivated by racial demographics rather than health risks. Furthermore, our results show an intense and uneven pandemic-related news surge in early 2021 that possibly contributed to the emergence of the Delta variant in the U.S. around the same period. This highlights the complex global interconnectedness of modern infectious disease outbreaks and the need for U.S. local disease control strategies to be globally aware. Ultimately, our study highlights the pandemic as a significant U.S. local news theme that raised questions about the media's role in shaping public perception and policy responses to public health issues in the age of misinformation. Using a media influences model, our analysis assesses the impact of local news COVID coverage on the area's case and death rates and their underlying mechanisms, which supports previous studies linking media reporting and public behavior. To combat future pandemics, our study recommends incorporating science and health professionals into local media to enhance public awareness and understanding of global public health issues. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide the robot through unexplored areas. An algorithm called HiTMapUpdate is also introduced for updating the map, involving a mechanism to eliminate drift by revisiting and correcting outdated information. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through simulation results showing significant reductions in navigation errors and impressive performance at scale with minimal computational demands. An accompanying video can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/hitmap. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/jaychuank/HiTMap. Following the successful testing of the system in simulation, a mobile robot was deployed in a large outdoor environment to put HiTMap into practice. The findings from this real-world experiment show that HiTMap meets all the essential criteria for a practical mapping system: efficient, accurate, and on par with state-of-the-art map representations. In addition to these achievements, HiTMap's mapped obstacles show promising results in assisting learning-based obstacle avoidance algorithms due to its unique representation. In the future, modifying HiTMap to accommodate more advanced learning-based navigation approaches could lead to significant advancements in autonomous navigation technologies. Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can be trained to tackle various clinical issues when provided with comprehensive, long-term patient data. The motivation behind this work stems from the current practice of medical professionals acquiring patient histories and previous medical records as a means to inform and improve their decisions. Similarly, developing a system that can provide informed recommendations to medical staff by analyzing patient data from a medical perspective is at the core of our research. In the context of graduate-level machine learning and computer science programs, we design a course centered around extracting clinical insights from EHRs and developing informative applications for medical staff. As part of this course, we employ a search-based optimization algorithm to improve the accuracy of diabetic blood sugar management predictions in patients. The outcome of this work involves the development of a comprehensive educational pathway grounded in real-world clinical relevance, demonstrating the value of extracting meaningful clinical insights from EHRs. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/dblanc/bda-mip. The knowledge gained from this experience has enabled us to extract two clinical applications, one predicting diabetes risk based on EHRs and another forecasting patients' response to anti-depressant medication. The clinical validity of these applications has been validated by a medical doctor. The remaining sections outline the creation of a graduate-level course focused on extracting clinical insights from EHRs and developing informative applications for medical staff, detailing the key decisions that drove our research choices, and presenting the results of our work using a search-based optimization algorithm to improve the accuracy of diabetic blood sugar management predictions in patients. The outcome of this work involves the development of a system that provides informed recommendations to medical professionals and the accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/dblanc/mip-floresv. The clinical validity of this application has been validated by a medical doctor and the insights gained have enabled us to forecast patients' response to anti-depressant medication. The final clinical application developed as part of this work has the potential to help mental health professionals in non-profit organizations, who face significant difficulties accessing the latest machine learning technology and expertise due to limited resources. The research presented in this work has been conducted at the intersection of machine learning and clinical medicine; a field where progress is inherently interrelated with other disciplines. The outcome of this research has a dual impact as it benefits both the academic community, showcasing the value of extracting meaningful clinical insights from EHRs, and the medical community, providing informed recommendations to medical professionals. , femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser changes their dynamics significantly, even if the X-ray intensity is very low. This is due to the interaction of the X-rays with the electronic excitations caused by the pulse's impact. We investigated the effects of varying X-ray intensity on the structural changes of a specific crystal, enstatite phosphate, when hit with X-rays of different intensities. The results show that for lower X-ray powers, the evaporation of electrons leads to the crystal changing its shape through thermal expansion after the X-ray exposure, while for higher X-ray powers, the electronic evaporation leads to collective ion movements, resulting in permanent crystal structure changes. Additionally, experiments and simulations reveal that the crystal modifications mainly happen in the surface layers. These findings demonstrate that the electronic interactions triggered by the X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser can cause notable solid-state transformations. This raises the possibility of using electronic excitations to induce changes in materials that were previously thought impossible. Furthermore, controlling the intensity of X-ray pulses allows for exploring new mechanisms of materials modification, such as multi-phased transitions, and the creation of unique nanostructured materials with properties not found in their original state. Ultimately, this research suggests that free-electron lasers can perform tasks similar to traditional methods of solid-state analysis, but with more features. This implies numerous potential applications, including, but not limited to, the generation of materials with tailored gradient compositions, the induction of phase transitions, and the creation of materials with unique nanostructured properties. Furthermore, experiments and simulations have revealed a novel phenomenon of reversible solid-state transformations, which could be applied to various materials and processing methods. This new category of free-electron laser processing holds significant historical significance as it redefines the approach to solid materials modification that was first introduced by Erwin E. Meyer in 1968. Additionally, the potential research avenues in this area are still available, providing a new starting point for experimental and theoretical studies of solid materials modification. This particular processing method also offers a perspective on overcoming the thermodynamic limit of transformation rates by utilizing dynamic changes to the crystal structure. Key aspects of this method include, but are not limited to, the induction of phase transitions, the creation of unique gradient-spotted materials, and the generation of gradient-layered materials. Moreover, the method raises questions and demonstrates the feasibility of overcoming the thermodynamic limit of transformation rates by utilizing dynamic changes to the crystal structure. This understanding provides a new point of comparison for evaluating the efficacy of free-electron laser processing

Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach specifically protects AMC systems from attacks like the Fast-Gradient Sign method. The existing GAN countermeasures were ineffective in our scenario, so we employed a new variant that uses the spectral norm constraint to improve its resilience against adversarial attacks, significantly outperforming simpler countermeasures in our simulations. This work is the first to our knowledge to address the issue of adversarial attacks in AMC and explore GAN-based countermeasures to mitigate them successfully in a DNN-based classification system. Even when the DNN is not normally trained on signals with adversarial noise, our approach successfully identifies the class of such signals, indicating that AMC remains robust against such attacks. Additionally, we found that the primary consideration when selecting a GAN-based countermeasure should be its ability to accurately classify any given signal, regardless of the type or source of adversarial noise. This countermeasure can be optimized using synthetic data generated from knowledge-acquired signal patterns, further simplifying its integration with AMC systems. We showed that the performance of our approach is comparable to that of AMC systems that aren't under attack in a variety of wireless channels, even when the only training data available is from a single class. Furthermore, we found that the reduced signal-to-noise ratio caused by the adversarial attack can be compensated for by using our approach. This countermeasure can be used in a variety of wireless channels, including both flat and frequency-selective channels, and we found that the significant performance gains seen in the flat channel also apply to the frequency-selective channel. This is likely due to the high bandwidth of the adversarial attack, which is assumed here to be greater than that of the actual signal. We found that the performance of our approach is consistent across a range of possible bandwidths for the adversarial attack. This countermeasure can be used in a variety of wireless channels, including both coherent and non-coherent AMC systems. We found that the performance of our approach is consistent with that of the coherent case having no adversarial attack and is comparable to, though not as simple as, the non-coherent case. Nevertheless, our investigation demonstrates that PINNs are susceptible to significant errors under conditions of data scarcity and artificial noise incorporation. Furthermore, we observe that these errors are rooted in the methods used for both PINNs and traditional neural networks. Conversely, our results show that incorporating noisy data enables neural networks to perform well even when data is scarce, a phenomenon we see for the first time. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect method of introducing noise to test data poses problems as it cannot be reversed and may lead to unreasonable constraints on the attack. Moreover, it may not successfully launch the attack as it underrepresents the impact of an attack. Our work focuses on direct attacks on graph classification by introducing labelled instances to training data to increase the likelihood of incorrect classification. We introduced a new method called LAD for labelled adversarial training which limits the number of added labelled instances and optimizes their placement using compression algorithms to increase the chances of successful attacks on given graph classifiers. We compared our method with existing test data perturbation based adversarial attacks to show their differences in performance, resources and scope. Our experiments using LAD on well known graph classification metrics and top 10 graph classification datasets from public libraries have shown that this method successfully launches attacks with a much lower number of added labelled instances compared to methods that introduce noise to test data. The implementation details are available on GitHub with the link: https://github.com/khawarfarooq/GraphClassificationAdversarialAttack. We also discussed the challenges and the future research scope of Graph Classification Adversarial Attacks. We also introduced our newly developed graph classification metric called Supported Label F1-measure to evaluate the performance of both the adversary and the defender to increase the scope of research in Graph Classification Adversarial Attacks. We verified that this metric has a significant correlation with the number of added labelled instances and compared the performance of different metrics on this benchmark to show their differences in performance. The use of LAD has the potential to expand the applicability of Graph Classification Adversarial Attacks and provide a more direct path to research in this area. We also discussed the direct method of introducing noise to test data as a degenerate case of labelled adversarial attacks where zero labelled instances are added which may seem to have a lower impact but can still effectively launch the attack.
